concept.name: Reversal conversion
concept.definition: A reversal (reverse conversion) is an arbitrage position consisting of short the underlying, short a put, and long a call at the same strike and expiration — short stock plus a synthetic long stock via options. It is the mirror image of the conversion, traded when the synthetic long is cheap relative to actual stock under put-call parity.
concept.intuition: You are short the stock and long its exact option-built replica; the two cancel into a fixed payoff, monetizing any small mispricing between the stock and its synthetic.
concept.mechanics: Short stock + short put + long call (same K, same expiry) has a constant expiration obligation/value of -K (the position is effectively short the strike). It is established when call-put prices imply a synthetic long cheaper than the actual stock; the position earns the deviation but requires borrowing the shares.
concept.formula: Expiration value = -S_T - max(K - S_T, 0) + max(S_T - K, 0) = -K; fair proceeds approximate PV(K) by put-call parity.
concept.failure_modes: Stock-borrow recall or buy-ins break the hedge and can force unwinds at a loss; assignment on the short put and changes in borrow fees or rates can each consume the thin margin. These are market-maker trades with razor-thin edges.
concept.misconceptions: A reversal is not a directional short: the option legs neutralize the stock exposure, so P&L comes only from pricing deviation and carry, not from the stock falling.
concept.example: Short 100 XYZ shares at $100, sell the $100 put for $4.00, buy the $100 call for $3.40: net proceeds $100.60 against a fixed $100 obligation at expiration, locking in $0.60 before borrow and financing costs.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
